title: Right-to-Left Writing Systems
description: An introduction to right-to-left writing systems and what they mean for the design of digital interfaces.

items.title: Right-to-Left Writing Systems
items.html:
What "right-to-left" means

Some of the world's widely used writing systems run from right to left. Examples include Arabic (العربية), Urdu (اردو), Persian (فارسی), and Hebrew (עברית).

In an RTL line, the first character sits at the right edge, the line ends at the left edge, and the next line begins on the right. Embedded numbers, punctuation, and Latin-script terms are ordered correctly by the Unicode bidirectional algorithm when the base direction is declared.

تُكتب العربية من اليمين إلى اليسار.

اردو دائیں سے بائیں لکھی جاتی ہے۔

فارسی از راست به چپ نوشته می‌شود.

עברית נכתבת מימין לשמאל.

Each example sentence says that the named language is written from right to left.

Implications for books and digital UI

RTL writing systems aren't just a render-time setting — they shape how readers expect content to be organised:

  • Books open and progress in the opposite direction — the first page sits on the right.
  • Tables, timelines, and ordered lists feel natural running right to left.
  • Embedded numbers, Latin terms, and punctuation need correct bidirectional ordering inside an otherwise RTL line.
  • Navigation chrome, progress indicators, and directional icons are typically mirrored.

Adapting digital interfaces to RTL

For an interface to feel native to an RTL reader, two things must happen:

  1. The content declares its direction — via the HTML dir attribute (or the equivalent at the application layer) — so the bidirectional algorithm lays it out correctly.
  2. The chrome is mirrored — typically via logical CSS properties (margin-inline-start rather than margin-left, text-align: start rather than text-align: left) and flipped directional icons.

Honouring the first without the second produces readable RTL content sitting inside an LTR shell. Doing both is what makes the interface feel native to a reader whose script runs right to left.
